item.title: Could Your Anxious Companion Be Out of Balance?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Pet anxiety may have physical, behavioral, and energetic dimensions. Chakras are a framework holistic practitioners use to understand what conventional training and medical care sometimes miss
  • The four foundation chakras most tied to anxiety are the root (safety), sacral (emotional connection), solar plexus (confidence), and heart (bonding). Imbalances show up as reactivity, shutdown, or clinginess
  • Animals also have two chakras humans don't: the brachial (human-animal bond) and the bud chakras in the paw pads, which is why bare-paw earth contact often visibly calms indoor pets
  • Pets mirror their humans' emotional states; dogs mirror intensity, while cats mirror tone, so regulating your own nervous system with slow breaths and calm presence often settles them too
  • Simple home practices support balance: predictable routines, consent-based touch, sound and color support, confidence-building activities, and quiet time, always used alongside veterinary care, not as a replacement

Your dog paces the same path across the living room floor. Your cat hides for hours after a visitor leaves. Bedtime feels less like winding down and more like managing another restless spell. Anxiety in pets has become one of the most common concerns pet parents bring up, and the usual toolbox — training, exercise, calming supplements, and veterinary care sometimes gets you most of the way there but not all the way.

What if there's another layer worth considering? A growing number of holistic practitioners suggest that anxious dogs and cats often have something more than a behavioral or medical issue at play. They may also be energetically out of balance.

The Energy Framework, Briefly

Chakras are described in traditional and integrative healing frameworks as spinning centers of energy that regulate how life-force energy flows through the body. Each chakra corresponds to specific physical, emotional, and behavioral qualities. When they flow smoothly, animals tend to feel balanced and calm. When they get stuck, depleted, or overworked, imbalances show up.

Modern research in biofield physiology has begun to describe the body as surrounded and interpenetrated by dynamic electromagnetic and subtle-energy fields that are measurable, responsive to the environment, and reflective of stress and regulation. Chakras fit within this emerging framework as organized centers within that field.

Just to say clearly upfront: Chakra work is not a replacement for veterinary care. Always rule out medical causes for behavioral changes first, and treat energetic support as a complementary layer, not an alternative to appropriate diagnosis and treatment.1,2

The Chakras That Most Affect Anxiety

Animals have the same seven main chakras as humans do, plus two more that exist only in animals. When it comes to anxiety, a handful of these energy centers do most of the work.3,4

  • Root chakra (base of spine and hindquarters) — This governs safety, grounding, stability, and survival needs. When it's unbalanced, animals often show fearfulness, hypervigilance, reactivity, excessive timidity, nervous toileting, resource guarding, or difficulty settling. Rescue animals often carry deep root depletion from prior instability.
  • Sacral chakra (lower abdomen) — This chakra rules one-on-one relationships, emotional expression, playfulness, and sensory comfort. Imbalance here often shows up as separation anxiety, shutdown, over-grooming, avoidance of certain kinds of touch, or compulsive patterns.
  • Solar plexus chakra (upper abdomen and diaphragm) — It's the home of confidence, personal power, boundaries, and digestion. When it's off, you may see submissiveness, chronic gut issues, people-pleasing behavior, irritability, or sudden emotional outbursts.
  • Heart chakra (center of the chest) — This chakra governs bonding, empathy, love, grief, and connection. Imbalance can look like separation anxiety, clinginess, withdrawal, grief-related shutdown, or difficulty forming new attachments.

Together, these four form what some practitioners call the foundation chakras: the energetic base layer of emotional wellbeing. Most anxiety-related patterns trace back to imbalances in one or more of them.

The Higher and Animal-Only Centers

Three more chakras — throat, third eye, and crown — govern communication, intuition, and higher awareness. Imbalances in these may show up as excessive vocalization, sudden silence, avoidance of collars or touch on the neck, or unusual sensitivity to environments.

Animals also have two unique chakras that humans do not. The brachial chakra sits in front of the shoulders and governs the energetic bond between animal and human. Sensitive animals with an overloaded brachial chakra often feel responsible for the household's emotional tone.

The bud chakras sit in the pads of all four paws and connect animals to the Earth. They help with navigation, grounding, sensing environmental change, and discharging stress. Indoor pets often become calmer and more centered with regular bare-paw contact with the Earth.5

Signs Something Is Out of Balance

Chakra work is one way to describe patterns that pet parents often already sense but cannot quite name. Signs that your animal's energetic system may need support include:

  • Fearfulness or avoidance without a clear trigger
  • Sudden behavioral shutdown or withdrawal
  • Digestive flare-ups during stressful times
  • Agitation in specific rooms or corners of the house
  • Clinginess with only one person
  • Compulsive licking, chewing, or grooming
  • Inability to settle or sleep
  • Intolerance to touch around certain body areas
  • Excessive vocalization or sudden silence
  • Restlessness without an obvious cause

These are not behavioral "faults" and are not something to punish or train out. From an energetic view, they are your animal's way of communicating that something in their system needs attention.

Emotional Mirroring: What Your Nervous System Is Doing

One of the more interesting themes across holistic practitioners is that pets often mirror the emotional state of the people around them. Dogs tend to mirror emotional intensity — if the household is high-energy and stressed, dogs often become high-energy and stressed as well. Cats often mirror emotional tone, absorbing the quieter but chronic states of the humans they live with.

This isn't blame. It's an invitation. When we regulate our own nervous systems, our animals often shift with us. A few deep breaths, softening your shoulders, and grounding your feet before you approach your anxious pet can settle both of you at once.

Practitioners point to well-documented research showing that pets exhibit measurable relaxation when exposed to calm, coherent human energy — and that the heart produces an electromagnetic field that extends well beyond the body and changes with emotional state. Whatever framework you use to describe it, the effect is real: your calm supports their calm.6

Gentle Ways to Support Your Pet at Home

You do not need to be a trained energy healer to help your pet's system come into better balance. Some of the most powerful practices are also the simplest. Consider these strategies:7,8

  • Regulate yourself first — three slow breaths, softening your shoulders, grounding into your feet. Animals feel the shift and often settle in response.
  • Create predictable routines — The root chakra thrives on stability. Consistent meal times, walk times, and bedtimes help your pet feel secure in their own life.
  • Use intentional, consent-based touch — Slow, gentle strokes along the spine, shoulders, and paws can help rebalance multiple chakras at once. Follow your pet's cues — if they lean in, keep going. If they move away, respect that.
  • Try earth contact — Whenever possible, let your pet walk barefoot outside on grass, soil, or sand. Bud chakras in the paw pads discharge accumulated stress and reconnect them to the ground. It's one of the reasons even a short garden visit often visibly settles an anxious dog.
  • Sound support may help — soft frequencies, humming, gentle instrumental music, or even quietly singing to your pet can help regulate their energetic body.
  • Try color associations — some practitioners suggest color-supported environments — red-toned bedding for grounding, orange or yellow for confidence, green for heart connection, purple for intuition. It costs nothing to experiment.
  • Do confidence-building activities — nose work, gentle training, puzzle feeders, and small challenges your pet can succeed at — to support the solar plexus chakra and reduce anxiety over time.
  • Strengthen the bond — Focused, unhurried quality time — brushing, gentle massage, quiet moments together — supports the sacral and heart chakras and reduces separation-related anxiety.

The strongest chakra medicine any animal has is your presence, your steadiness, and your intention.

When to Bring in a Professional

Some challenges benefit from deeper energetic support alongside your veterinary care. Reasons to consider working with a certified animal communicator, energy healer, or holistic vet include:

  • Trauma histories that run deep, especially in rescue animals
  • Chronic issues that persist without a clear medical cause
  • Behavior that has escalated beyond what training alone can address
  • Animals that seem to be carrying the emotional load for the whole family
  • End-of-life support, where energetic peace and comfort matter

Professional chakra work and animal communication are best used as a complement to your regular veterinary team, not a replacement. A good practitioner will help you identify where the imbalance sits, offer gentle ways to restore harmony, and coordinate with your vet when medical issues need to be addressed.

A Different Way to See the Situation

For pet parents who have tried every conventional avenue and still feel like something is off, chakra work offers a fresh lens. It reframes the question from "what's wrong with my pet" to "what does their whole system need right now?" It replaces the sense of a stubborn behavior problem with the sense of a communication signal, one that can be met with patience, presence, and gentle support.

The evidence base for energy work in animals is still developing, and skeptics will point out that not every claim in this space has been rigorously tested. That's fair. But the underlying instincts that animals feel our emotional states, that predictable routines settle nervous systems, that grounded human presence helps a scared dog, that touch and rhythm and consistency matter line up remarkably well with polyvagal research, biofield physiology, and everything we already know about how mammals co-regulate.9

The Bigger Picture

Your anxious companion may not be broken, disobedient, or in need of another training class. They may simply be a highly sensitive animal in a complicated world, doing their best to process a lot with a limited toolkit.

Chakra healing offers a way to think about anxiety that includes one's emotional and energetic reality alongside one's physical health. Whether or not the language of chakras fully resonates with you, the practices it points toward — steady routines, gentle touch, regulated humans, earth contact, quiet time, confidence-building, and connection are all things almost every anxious pet benefits from.

Start where you are. Rule out medical causes with your vet. Notice what your pet is asking for. Regulate your own nervous system, then offer them the same kind of steadiness in return. That combination alone often unlocks meaningful shifts. And if you need deeper support, there are experienced practitioners who can meet you and your animal exactly where you both are, gently helping bring things back into balance.

Sources and References

  • 1,7 Amy Lim Healing, How Can Energy and Chakra Healing Benefit Your Beloved Pets?
  • 2,4,5,6,9 Animal Communication For Healing, Understanding Your Pet's Chakra System
  • 3,8 Animal Wellness Magazine, August 14, 2026

item.title: Why Ear Problems Are Nearly Epidemic in Dogs
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Ear inflammation is common in dogs, and it often progresses to an ear infection that persists or recurs
  • Dogs with inflamed or infected ears tend to shake their heads a lot and scratch at their ears, and the ear canal is often red with an unpleasant odor
  • There are many potential causes for canine ear problems, including allergies, moisture in the ears, wax buildup, and foreign material in the ear canal
  • Ear infections in dogs can be fungal (e.g., yeast), or more commonly, bacterial
  • Preventing ear infections in your dog involves checking the ears daily, cleaning them as often as necessary and addressing changes in the ears immediately

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published May 20, 2020.

Ear infections are a common problem in many species of animals, but they’re a borderline epidemic in dogs, due in part to the way the canine ear canal is constructed.

For example, unlike human ears in which the internal canal is straight and horizontal, your dog’s ear canal is formed like an “L.” There are wax-secreting glands lining the canal, along with hair that moves the wax up and out, but the gunk has to execute a 90 degree turn before making its way to the outer canal.

A normal, clean canine ear canal is a healthy pink color with no unpleasant odor. When inflammation or infection is present, you may notice your dog shaking his head more than usual, scratching at his ears, or rubbing his head against the floor. When you go in for a closer look, you’ll probably notice the ear canal is red rather than pink, and there can be an unpleasant smell as well.

Chronic ear issues in dogs are a very common reason for veterinary visits. Inflammation or infection of the outer canal of the ear (called otitis externa) can be a frustrating, sometimes painful condition that almost always has an underlying cause (e.g., allergies).

Many chronic ear infections are ineffectively treated, and as a result, what appears to be repeated infections is actually a single infection that persists because it hasn’t been fully resolved.

There are two basic types of ear problems in dogs: chronic inflammation and infection. Untreated inflammation can lead to infection. If your dog's ears are warm to the touch, red, swollen, or itchy, but there's little to no discharge, chances are the problem is inflammation. However, if one or more of those symptoms is present along with obvious discharge, it's usually a sign of infection.

Causes of Ear Inflammation and Infection

  • Wax accumulation — A major reason for ear problems in dogs is wax buildup. The presence of earwax is normal, but dogs produce varying amounts. Some dogs need their ears cleaned daily, while others never develop a buildup. Certain breeds produce more wax than others, such as Labradors and other retrievers who tend to love the water.

    If you have one of these breeds, you should get your dog accustomed to having her ears cleaned while she’s a puppy. Other breeds that also tend to produce an abundance of wax are Bulldogs, Cocker Spaniels and Poodles.
  • Moisture in the ear — Another cause of ear inflammation is moisture, also known as “swimmer’s ear.” This is seen primarily during the summer months when dogs are outdoors playing in lakes.

    Wet ear canals and a warm body temperature are the perfect environment for inflammation and/or infection to occur. That’s why it’s important to thoroughly dry your dog’s ears each time he comes out of the water, has been outdoors in the rain or snow, and after baths.

  2. Organic apple cider vinegar mixed with an equal amount of purified water

  4. Green tea or calendula infusion (using cooled tea)
  5. One drop of tea tree oil mixed with 1 tablespoon coconut oil (for dogs only — never cats)
  6. Colloidal silver

A great method for cleaning most dogs' ears is to saturate a cotton ball with cleaning solution and swab out the inside of the ear. Use as many cotton balls as necessary to remove all the dirt and debris.

item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Romaine lettuce contains polyphenols that may support pet’s health in different ways, such as helping manage inflammation and immune system health
  • Research has shown that polyphenols in lettuce also help to regulate genes related to obesity and liver fat accumulation
  • Romaine lettuce also contains dietary fiber that may help keep your pet’s digestive health in top shape
  • Don’t feed too much romaine lettuce to your pet, as it may cause gastrointestinal upset due to excess fiber
  • While romaine lettuce can be a beneficial treat, it should be part of a rotation of fresh food treats within a species-appropriate diet

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published August 9, 2022.

When you think of salad, one of the first images that comes to mind is most likely romaine lettuce. It’s such a crucial component to this dish that it’s hard to imagine any salad bowl without romaine lettuce. That being said, you may be wondering if this crunchy vegetable can be an effective pet treat. It’s common to feed pets other vegetables for a midday snack, so why not romaine lettuce? Can the same benefits translate to them as well?

The answer is yes — your pet can enjoy the nutritional benefits of fresh, crunchy romaine lettuce, too. Read on to learn what experts have to say about the nutrients inherent in this vegetable.

Did You Know?

The word “lettuce” most likely comes from the Old French word “laitues,”1 which means milky. This refers to the milky sap coming out of the lettuce.2

Bioactive Compounds in Romaine Lettuce — Polyphenols

Around 90% of most lettuce varieties are made up of water, but that doesn’t mean there are no nutritional benefits. In fact, research has shown that lettuce is rich in polyphenols that may support animal health.3 One study published in 2009 found that increased polyphenol intake may help improve immune response in dogs. The researchers noted that canines that received polyphenols had altered gene expression related to leukocyte proliferation and signaling.4

Polyphenols may help better manage inflammation, according to research published in BMC Veterinary Research. The researchers also noted that polyphenols may help downregulate genes related to obesity and liver fat buildup.5

Regarding polyphenols’ potential to manage inflammation, the benefit may be especially pronounced in the digestive tract. Researchers suggest that increasing polyphenol intake may have a protective effect against gastrointestinal disease by controlling inflammation-related processes in the intestine. Polyphenols may also modulate the gut microbiome to lower the risk of digestive problems, most notably diarrhea.6

Romaine Lettuce Can Boost Your Pet’s Fiber Intake

Being a leafy vegetable, romaine lettuce contains ample amounts of fiber that may help promote better digestive health for your pet. The importance of fiber cannot be stressed enough, as it helps maintain a diversified microbiome and proper digestive functions, such as regular bowel movements. In a 2021 study, researchers noted that police dogs affected with diarrhea experienced lowered frequency of excrement, as well as better stool consistency, thanks to increased fiber intake. Furthermore, the dogs had an increase in mean body weight.7

Aside from keeping your pet on a regular pooping schedule, fiber may help keep more nutrients in your pet’s system. Research published in the Journal of Animal Science noted that an increase in fiber consumption led to a positive shift in fecal fermentative end-products, as well as a reduction of phenols and indoles in the feces itself.8

Romaine Lettuce Fun Fact

Ancient cultures have cultivated lettuce for thousands of years. Greeks, Romans and Egyptians all used and enjoyed lettuce to varying degrees in their cultures.9

How to Serve Romaine Lettuce to Your Pet

The best way to serve romaine lettuce to your pet is raw so they can get all of its benefits. Raw lettuce adds a unique texture to your pet’s meals. Another advantage to the raw approach is that it may help pets reach a healthy safe weight by keeping them satiated. In fact, the American Kennel Club recommends raw lettuce as a training treat for dogs that may need to lose weight.10 Shredded raw lettuce can be used as a topper for whatever food you’re currently feeding your pet.

When feeding lettuce to pets, it’s best to not feed excessive amounts, but you can easily add 1 to 2 tablespoons per cup of pet food, and some dogs enjoy a leaf by itself, as a snack. If you go overboard, your pet can experience loose stools, as too much fiber can cause stomach problems, including gas and bloating.11 You’ll know if your pet has the right amount of fiber if they’re producing small, firm stools.

Top Lettuce Growers in the World

China is the world’s top producer of lettuce, harvesting 14.32 million tons during 2020. The U.S. comes in second with 4.4 million tons. India takes the third spot with 1.12 million tons.12

A Look Into the Environmental Sustainability of Lettuce

While romaine lettuce may seem like an enticing snack for your pup, caution is advised whenever you purchase it from the grocery store. It’s highly likely that conventionally grown lettuce is contaminated with pesticides that may inadvertently affect your pet’s health. In fact, lettuce ranks 33rd in the Environmental Working Group’s 2026 Shopper’s Guide to Pesticides in Produce.13

In other news, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) also reported an E. coli outbreak in 2018 involving romaine lettuce, which affected consumers residing in multiple U.S. states. FDA investigators noted that the outbreak lasted for more than two months, causing people who consumed this lettuce to be hospitalized. It is believed that multiple environmental and processing factors caused the growth of the pathogens on the lettuce.14

With this information in mind, try to look for certified organic sources of lettuce. If it’s not possible to find spray-free lettuce, make sure to wash your vegetables thoroughly to remove as much pesticides as possible. Fresh snacks, even when grown conventionally, are still superior to feeding your pet entirely ultraprocessed snacks (made from conventional ingredients that most likely also have chemical residues).

For the best sustainability, grow your own lettuce. Lettuce can be easily grown throughout the year, even indoors.15 Done right, people living in urban areas with their pets can still get a steady supply of leafy greens and dedicate the saved money to other needs. Your local farmers market is also a great place to find fresh lettuce.

Romaine Lettuce Can Be a Crunchy Treat

Studies have shown that the bioactive compounds and fiber in romaine lettuce may contribute to better pet health. Romaine lettuce is a great crunchy treat for your pet, understanding that the bulk of their nutrition should still come from a species-appropriate, nutritionally complete diet. Rotate lettuce with other nutritious fresh food treats, remembering to wash your lettuce and other fresh fruits and veggies thoroughly to remove as many contaminants as possible.

Sources and References

  • 2 The Kitchn, What’s That White Sap in Romaine Lettuce? August 2, 2016
  • 3 Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety, Jan 2022, Volume 21, Issue 1, 4-45, 2.2 Polyphenols in Lettuce
  • 4 J Nutrigenet Nutrigenomics. 2009;2(1):43-52, Abstract

item.title: Alert Issued About Doggy Bad Breath: Never, Ever Do This
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • U.K. dog parents are being warned not to use human toothpaste when they brush their pet’s teeth to avoid exposing their dog to toxic ingredients
  • According to a survey of U.K. pet owners, many don’t realize the serious nature of dental problems in dogs, and think bad doggy breath is normal
  • Plaque and tartar buildup on your pet’s teeth can not only do irreversible damage to his oral health, but also to his heart health
  • Every dog parent should be aware of the 10 signs of dental disease
  • Steps you can take at home to help keep your dog’s mouth healthy include daily tooth brushing, feeding the right diet and offering recreational bones or high-quality dental chews

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published January 9, 2019.

In the U.K., the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (RSPCA) is warning pet parents not to use human toothpaste when they brush their dog’s teeth. The alert was issued “… after research suggested it was being seen as a solution to bad breath,” according to The Telegraph.1

The RSPCA cautioned that the presence of fluoride in many human toothpaste brands, along with the growing use of the artificial sweetener xylitol, could be toxic to dogs if ingested. It’s important to realize that unlike humans, dogs don’t spit out toothpaste, so every bit of it gets swallowed or absorbed through the tissues in the mouth.

In addition to fluoride and xylitol, most human toothpaste contains a long list of chemicals and other substances your dog (and you) may be better off avoiding. Recommendation is to use an all-natural enzymatic dental gel designed specifically for pets.

Survey Says: Lots of Dogs Have Halitosis, and Lots of Dog Parents Are Clueless

According to the Kennel Club, dental disease is the second most commonly diagnosed health issue for dogs in the U.K. In the U.S., it’s the number one medical problem — 80% of dogs have some degree of gum disease by the age of 3.

The RSPCA’s warning followed a survey of 2,000 pet parents that showed nearly 8% had tried to get rid of their dog’s bad breath with human toothpaste. Some people fed their dogs mints to freshen their breath, others offered sticks of gum and some thought a good grooming would solve the problem. There were even pet parents who vowed to keep their toilet lid down, fearing the time-honored canine tradition of drinking from the bowl was causing their dog’s stinky breath.

“While we applaud owners who take responsibility for caring for their dogs teeth, we would also stress that only toothpaste formulated for dogs should ever be used,” a Kennel Club spokeswoman told the Telegraph.

This is worth repeating. Regularly brushing your pet's teeth is the single most effective thing you can do to keep those teeth and gums in good condition. Daily brushing is ideal, but if that’s not workable, set a goal of four to five times a week.

Bad Breath Resulting from Gum Disease Isn’t ‘Normal’ for Dogs — It’s a Serious Problem

More than half the U.K. pet parents surveyed believed bad doggy breath was normal and not a symptom of poor dental health; only a fifth worried about bad breath being a sign of a serious health problem. When plaque isn’t removed from your dog’s teeth, it collects there and around the gum line and within a few days hardens into tartar. Tartar sticks to the teeth and ultimately irritates the gums. Irritated gums become inflamed — a condition known as gingivitis.

If your dog develops gingivitis, the gums will be red rather than pink and his breath will probably be noticeably foul-smelling. If the tartar isn’t removed, it will build up under the gums, eventually causing them to pull away from the teeth. This creates small pockets in the gum tissue that become repositories for additional bacteria.

At this stage, your dog has developed an irreversible condition, periodontal disease, which causes considerable pain and can result in abscesses, infections, loose teeth and bone loss.

When periodontal disease is present, the surface of the gums is weakened. The breakdown of gum tissue allows mouth bacteria to invade the bloodstream and travel throughout your dog’s body. If his immune system doesn’t kill off the bacteria, it can reach the heart and infect it.

Studies have shown that oral bacteria, once launched into the bloodstream, are able to fight off attacks by the immune system. What many pet parents don’t realize is there’s an established link between gum disease and endocarditis, which is an inflammatory condition of the valves or inner lining of the heart.

Researchers also suspect certain strains of oral bacteria may lead to heart problems. Some types of bacteria found in the mouths of pets produce sticky proteins that can adhere to artery walls, causing them to thicken. Mouth bacteria are also known to promote the formation of blood clots that can damage the heart.

How quickly these events take place depends on a number of factors, including your pet’s age, breed, genetics, diet, overall health, and the frequency and quality of dental care he receives. It’s also important to realize that some dogs will require regular professional cleanings even when their owners are doing everything right in terms of home care.

Signs of Possible Dental Disease in Your Pet

If you notice any of the following signs in your dog, it’s time to make an appointment with your veterinarian to prevent a dental problem from negatively impacting her health and quality of life:

  • Redness of the gums
  • Tenderness around the mouth and/or teeth
  • Bad breath
  • Drooling or dropping food
  • Loose teeth
  • Bleeding from the mouth
  • Discolored teeth
  • Loss of appetite/poor appetite
  • Broken teeth
  • Weight loss

5 Steps to Help Keep Your Dog’s Mouth Healthy

  1. Feed a nutritionally balanced, species-appropriate, fresh food diet, and feed it raw if possible. When your dog gnaws on raw meat, it acts as a natural toothbrush and dental floss.
  2. Offer recreational bones and/or a fully digestible, high-quality dental dog chew to help control plaque and tartar. The effect of dental chews is similar to raw bones, but safer for power chewers or dogs who have restorative dental work and can’t chew raw bones.
  3. Brush those teeth, preferably every day. If every day is too tall an order, commit to do it several times a week. A little time spent each day brushing your dog’s teeth can be tremendously beneficial in maintaining her oral health and overall well-being.
  4. Perform routine mouth inspections. Your dog should allow you to open his mouth, look inside and feel around for loose teeth or unusual lumps or bumps on the tongue, under the tongue, along the gum line and on the roof of the mouth. After you do this a few times, you’ll become aware of any changes that occur from one inspection to the next. You should also make note of any differences in the smell of your dog’s breath that aren’t diet-related.
  5. Arrange for regular oral exams performed by your veterinarian. He or she will alert you to any existing or potential problems in your dog’s mouth, and recommend professional teeth cleaning under anesthesia, if necessary.

Daily homecare and as-needed professional cleanings or nonprofessional dental scaling (NPDS) by your veterinarian or dental professional are the best way to keep your pet’s mouth healthy and disease-free. It’s important to note that while NPDS can be a great way to prevent dental disease from occurring, it’s not a good substitute in cases of moderate to severe dental disease.

Sources and References

item.title: Your Pup's Bath Schedule Might Surprise You
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • There is no one-size-fits-all bathing schedule for dogs, as their needs depend on breed, coat type, age, lifestyle, health, and the time of year
  • Bathing too often can wash away the natural oils that protect your dog's skin and coat, leading to dryness and irritation
  • Some dogs may need weekly baths, while others can go six to eight weeks or longer, depending on their coat, activity level, and individual needs
  • Seasonal changes can affect bathing frequency, with muddy spring weather, summer swimming, fall shedding, and dry winter air all influencing grooming needs
  • Regular brushing, spot cleaning, and fresh-water rinses can help keep your dog clean and maintain a healthy coat between full baths

Bathing your dog may seem like a simple part of pet care, but figuring out how often they need a bath is not always so straightforward. While many dogs do well with a monthly bath, the ideal schedule can vary from one pup to another.

Of course, keeping your dog clean is about more than a fresh smell. Baths remove dirt, debris, and dead hair that collect in the coat over time — and doing it on a regular basis helps support healthy skin in the process. For dogs of all ages, understanding their bathing needs goes a long way toward keeping them comfortable, clean, and feeling their best.

Why There Is No Universal Bathing Schedule

If you have ever asked fellow pet parents how often they bathe their dogs, you have probably received a variety of answers. Some swear by monthly baths, while others only reach for the shampoo when their dog starts to noticeably smell bad.

According to PetMD, there are no hard-and-fast rules for bathing frequency, because several factors influence how often a dog needs a bath.1 Beth Cristiano, owner of Pretty Paws LLC, shared a similar perspective in an American Kennel Club article:2

"How frequently a pet needs a bath greatly varies based upon their breed, lifestyle, length of coat, and how much homework a pet owner is willing to do."

This helps explain why two dogs living in the same home may have completely different bathing schedules. A dog that spends most of its time indoors may stay clean for weeks, while an adventurous pup who enjoys digging, hiking, and exploring muddy trails may need more frequent cleanup.

What Really Determines How Often Your Dog Needs a Bath

When it comes to bathing frequency, coat type is one of the biggest factors to consider. It is easy to assume that dogs with less hair need fewer baths and dogs with longer coats need more, but the reality is a bit more nuanced. Different coat types come with different grooming needs, which can affect their bath schedule.3,4

  • Hairless breeds — Dogs such as the Chinese Crested and Xoloitzcuintli may not have much fur, but they still require regular skin care. These breeds often need weekly baths to help maintain healthy skin.
  • Long-coated breeds — Dogs with longer coats typically need more brushing and coat maintenance to prevent tangles and mats. However, they do not always require more frequent baths. As groomer Jorge Bendersky explains, "For dogs with medium-to-large coats, a bath could be needed from weekly to every four to six weeks, as long as the coat is properly maintained in-between baths."
  • Corded breeds — Not all long-haired dogs need frequent baths. The Puli, for example, develops distinctive cords that require a different grooming approach. According to the Puli Club of America, "the Puli doesn't develop that typical doggie odor," and may not require as many baths as many other breeds.
  • Double-coated breeds — Breeds such as Labrador Retrievers, Golden Retrievers, and Siberian Huskies have coats that naturally help regulate temperature and protect the skin.

Your dog's coat type is not the only thing that affects how often they need a bath. Weather and seasonal changes can influence everything from how dirty they get to how their skin and coat respond to grooming. According to Earthbath, adjusting your bathing routine throughout the year can help keep your pup comfortable and their skin in good condition:5

  • Spring — This season brings mud, puddles, and a spike in environmental pollen, meaning allergens and debris can quickly build up in your dog's coat. Bathe your dog every four to six weeks during this time, using a soothing formula to calm irritated skin without over-drying.
  • Summer — The sunny season means more time outdoors — hiking, beach trips, and swimming — exposing your dog to bacteria, chlorine, and salt along the way. That is why a full shampoo bath about once a month is recommended, plus a clean water rinse after every outdoor swim to prevent irritation from sitting moisture and water contaminants.
  • Fall — Crispy leaf-season signals your dog's body to start growing a thicker coat for winter, often alongside a second shedding cycle. During this season, baths are best spaced out every six to eight weeks, to allow natural oils time to build up. Focus on thorough brushing to keep skin healthy.
  • Winter — The snowy season combines freezing outdoor air with dry indoor heating, creating ideal conditions for dry, itchy skin. That is why baths should be kept to a minimum — roughly every eight weeks. When necessary, use a hydrating conditioner to lock in moisture against the harsh air.

Age, Lifestyle, and Health Matter Too

While coat length and the time of year can have a big impact on your dog's bathing schedule, age, lifestyle, and health also deserve a spot in the conversation. Younger dogs often need more baths simply because they tend to be more active and get dirty more easily.6 Puppies under eight weeks of age, though, should not receive full body baths unless absolutely necessary because they are not able to regulate their body temperatures yet and are at high risk for hypothermia. Instead of a full bath, spot clean these very young pups with a warm washcloth.

Senior dogs, on the other hand, tend to be less active and may naturally stay cleaner for longer — but that does not mean their grooming needs are simpler. Mobility issues can play a role, as some older dogs need extra grooming support to stay clean when getting around becomes difficult. Some senior dogs may also develop health issues such as urinary incontinence, which can cause them to soil their coat more easily.

Dogs with chronic illnesses such as allergic dermatitis or Cushing’s disease often have compromised skin barriers and require more frequent bathing. If your pet has problems with skin health or recurrent skin, paw, or ear infections, talk to your veterinarian about bathing frequency and specialized or prescription shampoos. Depending on the medical situation, your pet may need bathing weekly or even more frequently than once per week.

Finding the Right Balance Between Baths

While baths play an important role in keeping your dog clean and comfortable, giving them too many can sometimes do more harm than good by washing away the natural oils that help keep their skin and coat healthy. Here are a few easy ways to help your pup stay clean between trips to the tub:7,8,9

  1. Make brushing a regular habit — One of the easiest ways to keep your dog's coat looking its best is through regular brushing. Besides removing loose fur, dirt, and debris, brushing can help prevent tangles and mats from forming. It also distributes natural oils throughout the coat, which helps maintain healthy skin and fur. For double-coated breeds, a soft brush works well for the topcoat, while a de-shedding tool helps manage the undercoat.
  2. Use spot cleaning between baths — Not every muddy paw print or grass stain requires a trip to the bathtub. Grooming wipes are perfect for quick wipe-downs of muddy paws, dirty bellies, removal of pollen from the coat, and tear stains after walks. For a more thorough refresh, a waterless foam can be massaged directly into a dry coat and brushed out to break down odor and detangle fur — no water needed.
  3. Rinse after swimming and outdoor adventures — During the warmer months, many dogs spend more time swimming, hiking, and exploring. While getting wet is not the same as getting clean, a quick rinse with fresh water can help remove chlorine, salt, or other debris that may linger on the coat after outdoor activities. A deodorizing spray can also help neutralize any lingering odors between full baths.
  4. Pay attention to changes in your dog's skin and coat — Dryness, excessive scratching, unusual odors, or changes in your dog's coat may be signs that their grooming routine needs adjusting. Some dogs may benefit from medicated shampoos and a specialized bathing schedule, so it is important to speak with your veterinarian if any skin concerns develop.

Finding the right bathing routine may take a little trial and error, but it does not have to be complicated. By considering your dog's lifestyle you can build a grooming routine that works for their individual needs. The goal is not to bathe your dog as often as possible. It is to keep them clean, so they are always ready for the next walk, cuddle, or adventure.

Sources and References

  • 1,3,6,7 PetMD, August 3, 2023
  • 2,4,9 American Kennel Club, February 23, 2023
  • 5,8 Earthbath, June 17, 2026

item.title: This 150-Pound Pig Runs the Entire House
item.description:
Lou has figured out exactly how to run her household. She squeals until breakfast arrives, nips at the dogs' tails, and refuses to take no for an answer. But this 150-pound troublemaker has a secret soft side — when she's scared, there's only one person she wants.
